# The household cascade on a machine with no GPU — the run

What was run on 2026-09-13, on this session's container, and what it
measured. The script is [`pipeline.py`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica-code/blob/main/docs/research/2026-09-13-voice-agents/notes/pipeline.py); the numbers below are
its printed output, from the third and final run (the first two died on a
truncated download and an API change, both recorded under *Traps*).

## The machine

Ubuntu 24.04 in a container, 4 vCPUs (Intel Xeon, 2.10 GHz), 15 GB of RAM,
no GPU. Python 3.12 in a virtual environment made with `uv`. No access to
Hugging Face; every model file came from a GitHub release.

## What was installed

`uv pip install kokoro-onnx silero-vad sherpa-onnx openwakeword soundfile`
on Python 3.12. The environment weighs **5.6 GB**, of which 3.2 GB is
NVIDIA's CUDA libraries and 1.2 GB is PyTorch — pulled in by `silero-vad`,
which depends on torch even when the ONNX model is used. The parts that do
the work are small: ONNX Runtime and sherpa-onnx.

| Package | Version | Note |
|---|---|---|
| `kokoro-onnx` | 0.6.1 | Kokoro 82M TTS on ONNX Runtime |
| `onnxruntime` | 1.30.0 | CPU provider |
| `silero-vad` | 6.2.1 | with `onnx=True`; drags in `torch` 2.14.0 |
| `sherpa-onnx` | 1.13.8 | three recognisers, one runtime |
| `openwakeword` | **0.4.0** | not 0.6.0 — see *Traps* |

Model files, all from GitHub releases:

| File | Size | From |
|---|---|---|
| `kokoro-v1.0.onnx` + `voices-v1.0.bin` | 311 MB + 27 MB | `thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx` release `model-files-v1.0` |
| `sherpa-onnx-whisper-tiny.en` (int8) | 245 MB (dir) | `k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx` release `asr-models` |
| `sherpa-onnx-moonshine-tiny-en-int8` | 120 MB (dir) | same |
| `sherpa-onnx-streaming-zipformer-en-2023-06-26` | 321 MB (dir) | same |
| `hey_jarvis_v0.1.onnx`, mel + embedding models | ~1.3 MB each | inside the `openwakeword` wheel |

## What it did

There is no microphone in a container, so the script makes its own
speech: Kokoro reads a sentence — "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy
dog, and the meeting moves to half past nine on Thursday." — and that
5.7-second clip, resampled to 16 kHz, is the input to everything that
listens. A second clip, "Hey Jarvis, what is the weather like today?", is
the input to the wake-word detector. Each stage is timed with
`time.perf_counter()`; the first call to a model is reported separately
from the second, because the first includes warm-up.

## The numbers

| Stage | Load | Work | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Kokoro** (`af_heart`, 24 kHz) | 0.99 s | 1.79 s for 5.70 s of audio — **RTF 0.31** (first call 1.82 s) | clean, natural sentence |
| **Silero VAD** (ONNX) | 0.07 s | 0.057 s for 5.7 s of audio | two segments: 0.0–2.6 s and 2.9–5.7 s, the pause at the comma |
| **whisper-tiny.en**, int8, offline | 1.15 s | **0.50 s** for 5.7 s (first call 0.52 s) | `The Quick Brown Fox jumps over the lazy dog, and the meeting moves to half past nine on Thursday.` |
| **Moonshine tiny**, int8, offline | 1.41 s | **0.29 s** for 5.7 s (first call 0.25 s) | `The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog, and the meeting moves to half past nine on Thursday.` |
| **Streaming Zipformer** (2023-06-26, chunk 16 / left 128), 100 ms chunks | 4.23 s | **18.3 ms of compute per 100 ms of audio** (worst chunk 95.7 ms); 0.18 s to flush after the last chunk; 1.23 s of compute for the whole clip | `THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG AND THE MEETING MOVES TO HALF PAST NINE ON THURSDAY` |
| **openWakeWord** `hey_jarvis` | 1.10 s | **3.46 ms per 80 ms frame** | best score 0.998; crossed 0.5 after 1.04 s of audio, i.e. as "Jarvis" ended |

Whole script, all stages, model loads included: 19.7 s wall clock, 35.6 s
of CPU time.

Reading the table:

- **The mouth is three times faster than real time** on four cores. A
  ten-word answer costs about a second to render, and Kokoro streams by
  sentence, so the first sentence plays while the second renders.
- **The ears are ten to twenty times faster than real time** for whole
  utterances. Whisper tiny's half-second on a 5.7-second sentence is the
  latency a cascade would add after the user stops speaking, before the
  LLM sees a word; Moonshine's 0.29 s is half that, at the same accuracy
  on this sentence. Both got every word; Whisper capitalised "Quick Brown
  Fox" as a title, which is the kind of thing its training data does.
- **Streaming changes what latency means.** The Zipformer spends 18 ms of
  every 100 ms chunk working and idles the rest, so the transcript is
  already complete, bar the last word, when the speaker stops. The 0.18 s
  flush is the tail latency. The transducer has no punctuation and no case
  — a downstream LLM does not care.
- **The wake word costs nothing.** 3.5 ms in every 80 ms, on one core,
  which is why the project's README can claim fifteen to twenty such
  models at once on a Raspberry Pi 3. It fired at the right moment on a
  synthetic voice it had never heard, which is also the project's point:
  the models were trained entirely on synthetic speech.
- **Add it up** for the cascade this article describes, with a local LLM
  in the middle: wake (free) → VAD (free) → STT (0.3–0.5 s after the last
  word, or ~0.2 s streaming) → LLM (whatever your model does; on this
  machine a 4B model would be the slowest stage by far) → TTS (~0.3 s per
  second of speech, streamed). The parts measured here sum to well under a
  second; the brain is the budget.

## What did not run

- **Anything hosted only on Hugging Face**: VoxCPM2, Pocket TTS, Moshi,
  Qwen3-TTS, Chatterbox, Kitten TTS, Smart Turn, the LiveKit turn
  detector, Kyutai STT. The Hub was unreachable from this session. Their
  speeds in the article are their READMEs' claims.
- **An LLM in the loop.** No text model was served, so there is no
  end-to-end voice-to-voice figure; the article's estimate is the sum
  above plus the reader's own model.
- **A GPU shape.** Nothing full-duplex or speech-native fits on a CPU
  container; Moshi's 24 GB and MiniCPM-o's 12 GB are quoted, not tested.
- **Real microphones, real rooms.** Synthetic speech, no noise, no echo,
  no accent. The recognisers' accuracy here says nothing about a kitchen.

## Traps

1. **A truncated download reads as a parser error.** The first
   `kokoro-v1.0.onnx` was 194 MB of 325 MB — a chained `curl … && …` had
   been cut off and the retry skipped the file because it existed. ONNX
   Runtime's message was `INVALID_PROTOBUF : Protobuf parsing failed`,
   which looks like a version mismatch. `Content-Length` against `ls -l`
   settled it in one line.
2. **openWakeWord 0.6.0 will not install on Python 3.12 on Linux**: it
   pins `tflite-runtime`, whose last wheel is for older interpreters, so
   `uv` silently resolved **0.4.0** (2023). The 0.4.0 API takes
   `wakeword_model_paths=[…]` and no `inference_framework` argument; the
   models ship inside the wheel. Two crashes to find that out. The
   detector itself works identically.
3. **The streaming transducer needs silence to finish the last word.**
   With 0.5 s of trailing zeros the transcript ended in `THURSD`; with
   1.0 s it ended in `THURSDAY`. A live system gets this from the VAD's
   end-of-speech, which is exactly what the VAD is for.
4. **`silero-vad` installs PyTorch and CUDA (4.4 GB) even for ONNX use.**
   sherpa-onnx bundles the same Silero model without torch; for a
   deployment, use that.
